title: "The Enemy Is at Honnō-ji": Did Mitsuhide Really Shout It? A Line Rewritten for 245 Years
description:
Night of Tenshō 10, 6th month, 1st day (June 20, 1582, Julian): Akechi Mitsuhide's army turns left at the Oinoyama fork, toward Kyoto. Stories today say he shouted "The enemy is at Honnō-ji" that night. Who first wrote it?

In order: the Shinchō Kōki, "via Yamazaki to Settsu"; Ōmura Yūko's Koretō Taiji Ki, just a march; Luís Fróis, a troop review, some suspecting Ieyasu; Honjō Sōemon (1640), "we just assumed it was Ieyasu"; the Kawasumi Taikōki, Saitō Toshimitsu aiming the units at Honnō-ji's grove. None has the line; that night left only Nobunaga's "ze hi ni oyobazu."

The earliest we've found: Hayashi Razan and son's Oda Nobunaga Fu (presented 1641; we read the 1658 print): soldiers ask at Ōeyama, Mitsuhide answers. Rai San'yō's Nihon Gaishi (sent to Matsudaira Sadanobu, 1827) moves it to the Katsura, whip raised; its source list names the Oda Nobunaga Fu.

Fróis and the Kawasumi Taikōki via Tokutomi Sohō, Honjō via Japanese Wikipedia; "earliest" is within our search. Why Mitsuhide rose is unsettled. Spoken dates are old-calendar; "I think" lines are this channel's view.

AI-generated illustrations; historical figures are cartoons, not likenesses; inside Honnō-ji is dialogue only.

As of 2026-10-20 (rewritten 2026-10-25 under new rules)

thumbnail.headline:
Mitsuhide
**shouted it?**
thumbnail.sub: The first book to write it: 59 years late

chapters.open-you: Night march: left at the fork

s001.text: You've surely heard it: "The enemy is at Honnō-ji."

s002.text: Japan's most famous line of treason; 300 years on, a Japanese idiom.

s003.text: Night of Tenshō 10, 6th month, 1st day: Mitsuhide leads his army out of Kameyama Castle.

s004.text: Not west: he turns east up Oinoyama. The road forks, right to Settsu, left to Kyoto. Mitsuhide goes left.

s005.text: Every story today has him shout that night: "The enemy is at Honnō-ji!"

s006.text: But the order Nobunaga's scribe wrote down wasn't that line.

s007.text: Stranger still: 59 years later, in a book presented to the shogun, a soldier asks him a question.

s008.text: This file follows the line 245 years to see how it was written.

s009.text: Who first wrote "The enemy is at Honnō-ji"?

s010.text: The man who wrote down that order was Nobunaga's own scribe, Ōta Gyūichi.

s011.text: His Shinchō Kōki is the most detailed record of its time; but that night, he wasn't there.

s012.text: He's exact to the day: 5th month, 26th, Mitsuhide enters Kameyama Castle; 27th, he draws lots on Mount Atago.

s013.text: The 28th, a renga gathering. Not a day missed.

s014.text: Night of 6th month, 1st: Mitsuhide tells only four top retainers: kill Nobunaga, take power.

s016.text: What he told the soldiers: via Yamazaki, march on Settsu.

s017.text: Picture yourself in that column: read the whole scroll, and that's all you hear: to Settsu.

s019.text: Four months later, Hideyoshi's writer Ōmura Yūko also made a record; it only has Mitsuhide march from Kameyama.

s020.text: Not one announcement; but it already brands Mitsuhide: no sudden impulse, but years of treachery.

s021.text: I should add: this was written by the winning side.

s022.text: Missionary Luís Fróis's report to the Church tells it another way; we read Tokutomi Sohō's Japanese version.

s023.text: Mitsuhide told the troops: Nobunaga wants to review us.

s024.text: But in the ranks, some grew suspicious: secret orders to go after Ieyasu?

s025.text: Tokutomi himself warns it's doubtful in many places.

s026.text: Three records, three versions, and none has "The enemy is at Honnō-ji." So what did the men in the column say?

s027.text: One man did tell. His name was Honjō Sōemon; in Kan'ei 17, in his eighties or nineties, he wrote about that night.

s029.text: The memoir's origin is unclear; it surfaced in 1930. We read a Japanese Wikipedia copy.

s030.text: So we treat it as one man's memory, not the rule.

s031.text: He wrote: we thought we were heading toward Yamazaki, but we were told Kyoto.

s032.text: Lord Ieyasu happened to be in Kyoto then; we just assumed it was Ieyasu.

s033.text: He also said: Honnō-ji? I didn't even know where it was.

s034.text: In your eighties, would you remember who you followed when young?

s035.text: He recalls following Saitō Toshimitsu's son all the way; Toshimitsu, one of that night's four top retainers.

s036.text: As they crossed the Katsura, dawn neared.

s037.text: Reading this, I thought: more than half a century later, he remembered not who the enemy was, but whom he followed.

s038.text: The next moment is in an earlier book: the Kawasumi Taikōki, written around the 1620s.

s039.text: Tokutomi Sohō says it records an officer's own experience. What did that officer hear?

s040.text: It says past the Katsura, the order passed down: from today, our lord is master of the realm; even sandal bearers must rejoice.

s041.text: But notice: this order still has no "enemy," nor Honnō-ji.

s042.text: So when was Honnō-ji finally named?

s043.text: Nearing Kyoto, Toshimitsu ordered: open the ward gates; units advance.

s045.text: Head for the grove at Honnō-ji.

s046.text: Picture Kyoto just before dawn: the ward gates pushed open one by one, each unit heading for that grove.

s047.text: Only at Kyoto's gates was Honnō-ji pointed out; but with no "enemy," and not by Mitsuhide.

s048.text: Nor can we say the soldiers never knew whom they'd attack.

s049.text: At that moment, Nobunaga was staying at Honnō-ji, with only 20 or 30 attendants.

s050.text: Days earlier, coming to Kyoto, he told his army: this time, don't follow.

s051.text: Think about it: an army of over ten thousand against 20 or 30 attendants. Any suspense left?

s053.text: Nobunaga first thought servants were brawling; at war cries and gunfire: who rebels?

s054.text: Mori Ran: Akechi's men. Nobunaga, in four characters: ze hi ni oyobazu.

s055.text: We read it as: it's come to this; nothing to say.

s056.text: Here's the odd part: the one line left from the temple that night is Nobunaga's, not Mitsuhide's.

s057.text: That day, Tenshō 10, 6th month, 2nd day, Nobunaga died at the temple.

s058.text: None of those records has Mitsuhide's line. So who first wrote it into a book?

s059.text: The earliest we've found: that book presented to the shogun, the Oda Nobunaga Fu.

s060.text: It notes: by the shogun's order, begun early 11th month, presented 12th month, 7th day.

s061.text: A whole book in just over a month. That was Kan'ei 18, 59 years after that night, a year after the old soldier's memoir.

s062.text: Signed by the shogunate's Confucian scholar Hayashi Razan, noting: drafted by his son Shunsai.

s063.text: It calls Ieyasu "Daigongen": a father and son writing Oda history for the Tokugawa.

s064.text: Think about it: writing Oda history for the Tokugawa, how do you handle Mitsuhide?

s065.text: Sadly, the copy presented to the shogun, we haven't seen;

s066.text: we read the edition printed in Kyoto 17 years later, in Meireki 4.

s067.text: How does it tell that night?

s068.text: Here, omens come sooner: at the renga gathering before marching, Mitsuhide suddenly asks: how deep is Honnō-ji's moat?

s069.text: He ate chimaki, leaves and all.

s070.text: Ever forgotten to unwrap one? Probably not.

s071.text: Neither of these is in the Shinchō Kōki's renga gathering.

s072.text: Then Mitsuhide secretly summons retainers at Kameyama Castle. Remember the four top retainers? Here, they're five.

s074.text: He asked: will you die for me? If not, cut off my head.

s075.text: Toshimitsu first said no; Akechi Samanosuke: it's been said; it will get out.

s076.text: Then Mitsuhide gave his reason: Nobunaga means to kill me.

s077.text: Marching out, he ordered: Kyoto tomorrow morning; let Nobunaga see our troops.

s078.text: The review the missionary heard of: here too.

s079.text: At Ōeyama, the puzzled soldiers asked: where are we really going?

s083.text: In the books we found, this is the first time it has a speaker, a place, and listeners.

s084.text: Did you notice? Someone asks first; then he speaks.

s085.text: Over 180 years later, the same scene was written again.

s086.text: The writer: Rai San'yō, in the Nihon Gaishi.

s087.text: In Bunsei 10, 5th month, he wrote to Matsudaira Sadanobu: 20-plus years on this book, kept in a chest, unshown.

s088.text: Sadanobu sent for it. Something you spent half your life on: who would you show first?

s089.text: Does his telling of that night match the Hayashis'?

s090.text: In his telling, the pretext changes: not a troop review, but orders west to aid Hideyoshi.

s091.text: At night, he crosses Ōeyama and reaches Oinosaka.

s092.text: Remember the opening fork? This book says: right is the road to Bitchū.

s093.text: Mitsuhide turns left; his soldiers are startled.

s094.text: This time, did a soldier ask?

s095.text: No one asks. The army crosses the Katsura, the river the old soldier crossed near dawn.

s096.text: Mitsuhide raises his whip, points east, and cries out:

s097.text: "My enemy is indeed at Honnō-ji!" My enemy, at Honnō-ji.

s098.text: The renga line, "how deep is Honnō-ji's moat," is here too.

s099.text: Even "at last they knew: rebellion" nearly matches the Oda Nobunaga Fu.

s101.text: Remember the 1641 book? It put the line at Ōeyama; here, it moves to the Katsura.

s102.text: And an answer becomes an announcement.

s104.text: But is there a thread linking the two books?

s105.text: The Nihon Gaishi's list of sources includes the Oda Nobunaga Fu.

s106.text: Did San'yō himself make it? We didn't find out; so it's only circumstantial.

s107.text: Same volume: Mitsuhide asks if his men will die for him, and says: Nobunaga nearly killed me many times.

s108.text: "Nobunaga means to kill me" is already in the Oda Nobunaga Fu; San'yō didn't invent that self-defense plea.

s109.text: His main change: the line's scene.

s110.text: I think that scene is just what a line needs to become famous.

s111.text: Think about it: an answer drawn out by a question, or a cry with a raised whip. Which would you remember?

s112.text: Later, the Nihon Gaishi was the most-read history from late Edo to Meiji.

s113.text: Meiji-era editions alone: over 20 in the Diet Library print this line.

s114.text: Open any one of them, and it's the whip version.

s115.text: So where did Mitsuhide's whip line end up?

s116.text: It entered everyday Japanese: by Meiji 28, a book was already using it as an idiom,

s117.text: meaning: the real target lies elsewhere.

s118.text: 20 years later, even a book on world politics used it: the real enemy is Britain.

s119.text: Today in Japanese, it needn't mean Honnō-ji.

s121.text: Meiji textbooks and popular histories kept both versions: some the Q&A, some the whip and the shout.

s122.text: One from Meiji 25: Mitsuhide raises his whip and shouts. A Meiji 35 textbook: the men ask, then he answers.

s123.text: One line, now with two dads.

s124.text: I think it's fitting: even this line's real author lies elsewhere.

s125.text: So who wrote "The enemy is at Honnō-ji"?

s126.text: It's a line written later. The earliest we've found: Hayashi Razan and his son.

s127.text: Remember the record that branded Mitsuhide just four months after?

s128.text: Over 400 years on, grudge, ambition, the Shikoku situation: so many theories that someone sorted them into 50 types. None is settled.

s129.text: Letters released in 2014 drew notice to the Shikoku theory, but don't say outright why Mitsuhide rose.

s130.text: So: the line, filed. The motive: still an open case.

s131.text: Where did you first hear this line? Tell me below.

s132.text: This channel sticks to the records. Subscribe to open the files with me.
